analysis.one_liner: Eliminates all federal income tax on capital gains starting in 2005.
analysis.headline: The bill to eliminate capital gains taxes drew no cosponsors and died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the tax code to allow a 100% deduction for all net long-term capital gains, wiping out federal income tax on profits from selling stocks, real estate, and other assets starting in 2005 [S3]. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote [S5]. It drew zero cosponsors [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large investment portfolios would gain the most. The bill would allow a 100% deduction for all net long-term capital gains starting in tax year 2005, effectively eliminating federal income tax on profits from selling stocks, real estate, businesses, and other assets held long-term [S3]. Anyone who sells appreciated assets benefits, but the size of the benefit scales directly with the size of the gains, which are concentrated among the wealthiest households. Trusts, estates, partnerships, S corporations, mutual funds, and real estate investment trusts also receive special coordinating rules under the bill [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would make every dollar of long-term capital gain deductible from gross income, so sellers of appreciated assets would owe no federal income tax on those profits starting in 2005 [S3].
It includes transition and special rules so that the tax-free treatment applies cleanly through mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, S corporations, partnerships, estates, and trusts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would bear the cost: every dollar of profit from selling stocks, real estate, businesses, and other assets held more than a year would become tax-free starting in 2005 [S3]. Because capital gains are realized overwhelmingly by higher-income households, the lost revenue would otherwise have been paid mostly by those at the top, and general revenues would have to cover government obligations instead.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury, funded by all taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The benefit is largest for those with the largest gains: a 100% deduction on net capital gains eliminates tax in proportion to the profit realized, and capital gains are realized overwhelmingly by higher-income households, so the tax relief would concentrate at the top [S3].

The bill repeals the entire existing capital gains rate structure, including section 1(h), with no replacement revenue, leaving the federal government forgoing all long-term capital gains receipts after 2004 [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would flow overwhelmingly to households that realize large capital gains, which are concentrated among the wealthiest Americans, while the cost would fall on the Treasury and, ultimately, on all taxpayers who make up the difference through other taxes or borrowing [S3]. Even a supporter would acknowledge that a zero rate on all gains makes the tax system more regressive and could encourage tax-avoidance structuring of income as capital gains. The bill offered no offsetting revenue and received no cosponsors, suggesting little appetite for it even in a Congress that cut capital gains rates elsewhere.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: The bill would have allowed a 100% deduction for all net capital gains, effective for tax years ending after December 31, 2004, repealing the separate capital gains rate structure in section 1(h) of the tax code [S3].
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction and no further action was ever recorded for the remainder of the 107th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors in the House [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off because the bill died: no revenue would have been lost to a full capital-gains tax holiday for the wealthiest asset holders. Wealthy investors lose the opportunity for a zero rate on asset sales that the bill would have created starting in 2005.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy asset holders, since the bill died

for.name: Rep. Joe Scarborough
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate taxes on net capital gains after 2004 and it was referred to committee [S5].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 28, 2001 and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee that received the bill, never scheduled it for a markup or floor consideration; the chair's identity is general public knowledge, while the inaction is shown by the bill's action history [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; the sole sponsor was a Republican and the bill drew no cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.note: Eliminating tax on capital gains would be worth the most to households with the largest investment portfolios, since the benefit is a percentage of gains realized. This is a direct transfer of tax burden away from concentrated wealth and toward the general taxpayer.

The bill includes detailed special rules for mutual funds, REITs, partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts, ensuring the tax-free treatment flows through these vehicles cleanly [S3]. Easier tax-free fund distributions could support the funds business, though the bill repeals some existing fund tax preferences.
